title: How Pacifism Works (And Could It?)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore pacifism: its etymology and history from Gautama Buddha and Ashoka through early Christianity, Quakers and Mennonites in colonial America, the nineteenth-century peace movement, and World War I conscientious objectors. They cover the just war theory and its six conditions, discrimination and proportionality, civilian casualties in modern war, and the many types of pacifism (absolute, conditional, pragmatic, fallibility, collectivist, technological, nuclear, ecological, selective). They discuss Gandhi's nonviolent resistance, conscientious objection in World War II, Vietnam, and Iraq, Denmark's resistance to Nazi occupation, the death penalty debate, and whether pacifism can work against groups like ISIS. The episode closes with a listener email from Dallas Cowboys guard Emmett Cleary about CTE and NFL player brain health.

segments.title: Blue Apron sponsor read and opening banter
segments.summary: Blue Apron meal kit sponsor read, followed by hosts' casual banter about patterns, the movie Steve Jobs, and the episode topic.

segments.title: Definition and early history of pacifism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether they'd call themselves pacifists, the Latin origin of the word, and the term's coinage around an 1906 peace conference. They trace early pacifism through the Buddha, the Buddhist king Ashoka, the Stoics, Jesus, and the early Christian martyr Maximilian.

segments.title: Gandhi, Renaissance humanism, and colonial Quakers
segments.summary: The hosts note that Gandhi supported some violence and was a pragmatic pacifist. They discuss Erasmus and Renaissance humanism, and Mennonites and Quakers in colonial America, including Pennsylvania's antislavery stance and the Quakers' treatment during the Revolutionary War.

segments.title: Napoleonic Wars, peace societies, and the Civil War dilemma
segments.summary: Bloody Napoleonic Wars and the unpopular War of 1812 fueled the nineteenth-century peace movement. The Civil War posed a dilemma for pacifists over slavery, and Angelina Grimké said war was better than slavery.

segments.title: Arthur Ponsonby and the just war theory
segments.summary: The hosts quote pacifist Arthur Ponsonby on war. They explain that the just war theory, beginning with St. Augustine and the Holy Roman Empire, allowed justified war, and list its six conditions: just cause, proper authority, good intention, last resort, likely peace, and proportionality of good over evil.

segments.title: Discrimination, proportionality, and civilian casualties
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the just war rules of discrimination and proportionality. They cite a UNICEF figure that civilian deaths rose from about five percent of war casualties at the start of the twentieth century to a much larger share by the nineties, and attribute this to urban battlefields and bombing campaigns such as the firebombing of Japan and German cities in World War II.

segments.title: Types of pacifism and the pacifism spectrum
segments.summary: The hosts describe a spectrum from absolute pacifism to conditional pacifism, with subtypes: pragmatic, fallibility, collectivist, technological, selective, nuclear, and ecological pacifism. They discuss positive peace and diplomacy, and the difference between personal belief and justification.

segments.title: Death penalty and personal moral struggle
segments.summary: The hosts discuss their personal feelings about the death penalty, compassion for people on death row, and how some crimes lead to a desire for vengeance. They describe the difficulty of these views.

segments.title: Conscientious objectors in World War I
segments.summary: The hosts describe conscientious objection in World War I, the white feather campaign in Britain, and the Richmond Sixteen, who were sentenced to death, commuted to hard labor, and put to breaking rocks in a Scottish quarry. They also describe Evan Thomas in the US and Ernest England in Britain.

segments.title: Conscientious objectors in World War II, Vietnam, and Iraq
segments.summary: The 1940 Selective Service and Training Act allowed noncombat roles for objectors, including the Civilian Conservation Corps and medical experiments such as the University of Minnesota starvation experiment. The Vietnam-era law required religious grounds, and about 170,000 were granted status. In 2004, 110 soldiers in Iraq filed for objector status.

segments.title: Gandhi's nonviolent resistance and Denmark under Nazi occupation
segments.summary: Gandhi's satyagraha is described as a pragmatic, weaponized form of nonviolence, with three levels of nonviolent resistance. The hosts then discuss Denmark's nonviolent resistance to Nazi occupation, in which Danish Jews were hidden and none died in the Holocaust.

segments.title: Poll hookers, self-defense, and ISIS
segments.summary: The hosts discuss common challenges to pacifism, including the argument that pacifists benefit from others fighting wars, and hypothetical defense-of-family scenarios. They close by asking whether pacifism works against groups like ISIS.

segments.title: Listener mail: CTE and NFL player brain health
segments.summary: Hosts read an email from Dallas Cowboys guard Emmett Cleary about player awareness of brain trauma and CTE risk and his views on the NFL's handling of head injuries.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and contact information and close the show.
